data_section_full_text:
4        Data

                       The data come from several sources. The financial data are from CRSP and Compustat,

                   the data on executive compensation and CEO tenure are from Equilar and BoardEx,17 and

                   data on restatements are from Audit Analytics. I use restatements that correct accounting

                   errors as a measure of detected misstatements. Table 1 provides the variable definitions.

                       I restrict my sample to CEOs who do not manipulate at the end of the year before



                   they join the sample. This no-manipulation restriction is tricky because CEOs can have

                   multiple episodes of manipulation that can go undetected. We might reasonably assume,

                   however, that external auditors involved in restatements make accurate judgments about

                   the years affected by manipulation, and therefore the end of the year before the restated

                   period and the end of the last restated year satisfy the no-manipulation restriction. These

                   cases cover CEOs who start in my sample the year before the first restated year or, if

                   the misreporting began before SOX, the year after the last restated year. The number of

                   these CEOs depends on the restatement selection criteria. I also include CEOs who join

                   their respective firms after SOX.18 The total number of CEOs in the final sample ranges

                   from 1,136 under the most restrictive restatement selection criteria to 1,243 under the least

                   restrictive criteria, spanning eight years between 2003 and 2010.

                       Whereas, in the model, manipulation is chosen by the manager, not all restatements
                       17
                          Equilar Inc. collects data on executive compensation from annual proxy filings (DEF 14A). Its coverage is more
                   than double the coverage of Compustat ExecuComp. Equilar provides a CEO’s resignation date but not the date on
                   which the CEO leaves the firm. These two dates can differ, for instance, because the CEO resigns but remains with the
                   firm as a member of the board. I obtain the date on which the CEO leaves the company from BoardEx, which provides
                   employment histories of individual executives.
                       18
                          Although the former CEOs constitute only 10% of the sample, the restatements by the firms they manage consti-
                   tute 70% of restating firms.

correct intentional manipulation. Although some discretion is unavoidable, having dif-

                   ferent definitions of an intentional misstatement helps address this issue. This choice re-

                   flects a trade-off between the likelihood of these restatements correcting intentional mis-

                   statements and the number of restatements. For instance, requiring a restatement-related

                   regulatory investigation reduces the number of restatements to a few cases, rendering es-

                   timation of the model infeasible. Instead, this paper adopts a broader definition based

                   on the types of accounting errors corrected by a restatement. Following Scholz [2008],



                   I consider three groups based on the significance of errors to investors from the least to

                   the most severe [e.g., Palmrose et al., 2004, Scholz, 2008]: restatements of revenue recog-

                   nition or core expenses errors, constituting 128 cases or 10.30% of firms; restatements of

                   revenue recognition or serious core expenses errors, constituting 103 cases or 8.64% of

                   firms; and restatements of revenue recognition errors only, constituting 61 cases or 5.37%

                   of firms.19,20

                       For all restatements, I require that misstatements occur within a CEO’s tenure and

                   have a nonzero net income effect in the first restated year. In the estimation, I set the

                   bias in book value equal to the cumulative impact of a restatement on net income and,

                   accordingly, the bias in earnings equal to the impact of a restatement on net income in a
                      19
                          Errors related to core expenses include the following: depreciation, depletion, or amortization errors (1); expense
                   recording (payroll, SG&A, other) (7); deferred stock-based or executive compensation errors (17); deferred stock-based
                   SFAS 123-only subcategory (39); lease, leasehold, and FAS 13-and-98-only subcategory (42); liabilities, accounts payable,
                   reserves, and accrual estimate failures (12); cost of sales (inventory and vendor) (20); and capitalization of expenditures
                   errors (23). Scholz [2008] documents a significantly negative market reaction on the restatement announcement date
                   only for the following: cost of sales (inventory and vendor) (20); liabilities, accounts payable, reserves, and accrual
                   estimate failures (12); and capitalization of expenditures (23) errors. Audit Analytics restatement category keys are in
                   parentheses.
                       20
                          Around 65% of restatements in each group are “Big R” or reissuance restatements that require the reissuance of
                   the financial statements and are disclosed on the Form 8-K, Item 4.02 [Whalen et al., 2015].

given year. The internet appendix provides details on restatement data.

                      Table 2 shows a fraction of firms restating each year and the magnitudes of bias in

                   book value and earnings by year. The fraction of firms misstating earnings in each year

                   declines over time because of the backward-looking nature of restatements and a general

                   declining trend in the number of restatements since the peak in 2006 [Whalen et al., 2015].

                   While the fraction of misstating firms declines, no discernible trend occurs in the bias.

                   Among restating firms, the mean bias in book value ranges from $2.17 million or 0.79%



                   of lagged total assets for revenue recognition errors to $3.54 million or 0.69% for rev-

                   enue recognition or core expenses errors. The corresponding bias in earnings ranges from

                   $1.42 million or 0.40% of lagged total assets to $2.10 million or 0.47%. Other character-

                   istics associated with restatement severity are the market reaction to restatement-related

                   disclosures and the number of years and errors restated.21 The value-weighted cumula-

                   tive size-adjusted return on all restatement-related disclosure days ranges from −1.58%

                   for revenue recognition errors to −2.20% for revenue recognition or core expenses errors.

                   The mean number of years restated is close to one and a half years, with a median of one.

                   The mean number of errors restated is close to two and a half, with a median of two.

                      This paper considers a linear contract that includes cash- and equity-based compen-

                   sation. The survey of CEO compensation by Frydman and Jenter [2010] documents that

                   most CEO compensation packages contain salary, bonuses, payouts from long-term in-

                   centives plans, and restricted option and stock grants. My specification of CEO compen-

                   sation captures salary and payouts from bonuses and long-term incentive plans in the
                     21
                          The internet appendix reports restatement characteristics.

cash component, and option and stock grants in the shares of equity. I focus on manip-

                   ulation incentives from stock and option grants, because they constitute a major part of

                   the CEO compensation [Frydman and Jenter, 2010]. To incorporate the non-linearity of

                   option payoffs, I use option’s delta to convert option grants to effective equity shares.

                   Because CEOs’ nonfirm wealth is unobserved, I compute a CEO’s cash wealth at the be-

                   ginning of the first year as a multiple η of his firm-specific wealth in the first year setting

                   η = 1.22,23



                       Table 3 provides descriptive statistics for the variables and firm characteristics. Be-

                   cause the CRRA utility specification allows the rescaling of a CEO’s wealth without af-

                   fecting the optimal manipulation decision, I rescale variables as described in Table 1 and

                   denote them by lower-case letters. The significant variation in cash wealth, equity hold-

                   ings, and CEO age suggests potential variation in optimal manipulation decisions across

                   CEOs. As for the stock prices, I assume firms in the same industry are likely to have simi-

                   lar investment opportunities, technologies, and markets and thus have a similar evolution

                   of the intrinsic stock price process and earnings response coefficients. Accordingly, these

                   parameters are estimated within the industries defined using Standard & Poor’s Global

                   Industry groups. The firms in my sample are comparable in size to a generic Compustat

                   sample.24
                      22
                          I also examine η = 0.5 and η = 1.5 [similar assumptions are made in Hall and Murphy, 2002]. An alternative ap-
                   proach is to compute CEOs’ nonfirm wealth using an estimate of accumulated past CEO compensation as in Dittmann
                   and Maug [2007]. Estimates in Table 1 from Dittmann and Maug [2007] imply η = 0.54 for median values of wealth
                   and equity holdings.
                       23
                          In the sample, the mean cash wealth is $26.46 million, and the value of equity holdings is $22.84 million. The
                   internet appendix reports descriptive statistics for the dollar value of CEO wealth.
                       24
                          The mean firm assets are $4.1 billion, a number approximately 1.2 times larger than the mean of all firms in
                   Compustat over the same period.
review_notes: Section 6.1.2 identifies revenue recognition errors as the preferred Table 4 specification for subsequent interpretation. Its 1,136 CEOs are the primary N. The two broader criteria remain listed as other Table 4 estimates.
